activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
The rink had emptied an hour ago, but nobody in the lobby wanted to leave. A television had been wheeled out from the office and propped on two folding chairs, and around it sat Kayla's whole family plus half the neighbours, coats still on, watching the World Cup. The Zamboni had gone quiet in the background. Through the double doors Kayla could see the ice, pale and flawless, waiting for a public skate that would not start for another ninety minutes.

Peter had claimed the good couch by the vending machines. Genevieve sat cross-legged on the floor beside him, working through a bag of salt and vinegar chips, and Kayla's father stood at the back with his arms folded, radiating the particular tension of a man whose team was up by one with four minutes left. Kayla herself sat on the rubber mat by the skate rental counter, close enough to the TV to feel its warmth, far enough from her father that she could pretend not to watch his hands.

The equalizer came in the eighty-eighth minute. A corner, a scramble, a shin pad, and then the ball bulging the net while half the lobby roared and the other half groaned. Peter was on his feet with his jacket half off, spinning it over his head like a lasso, and Genevieve was laughing at him, and Kayla's father had turned away to face the dark rink as though the glass itself had personally betrayed him.

Then the referee made the box signal with his hands and pointed to his ear, and everything stopped.

"What's happening," Genevieve said. She said it flatly, the way she asked questions when she suspected the answer would be boring.

"They're checking the goal," Kayla said. "VAR. It's the first World Cup with it. They used video assistant referees in Russia this year." She had read an entire article about it on the bus that morning, partly because the article was there and partly because she had wanted something to hold in her mind other than the acceptance letter folded into her back pocket, the one she had not yet shown her father.

"So they can just take it back?"

"If it was offside, or a foul. They review goals, penalties, red cards." Kayla paused, hunting for the last item. "Mistaken identity, too. If they book the wrong player."

"Like when the ref gave Mr. Pritchard's kid a penalty that was obviously the other one," Peter said. Mr. Pritchard, who taught chemistry and coached the rink's Sunday league, was sitting near the doors in his rink-issue jacket, and he lifted a hand as though conceding the point without comment.

"Exactly like that," Kayla said.

Nobody moved during the check. The commentary murmured, the lines replayed, and Kayla found herself studying her father's back. He was watching the dark ice now, actually watching it, and she remembered being nine years old on that same ice, gripping the boards with both hands while he stood a few metres away, patient as a fence post, waiting for her to let go on her own. She had refused for two full sessions. On the third, she pushed off without telling him, and he didn't cheer or clap, he just skated alongside her, matching her wobble, saying nothing, and it was the safest she had ever felt.

The screen showed the freeze-frame again. A shoulder, a line drawn across the pitch, a margin so thin the commentators were arguing about pixels. Kayla began to ruminate on the whole idea of it, how a stadium of eighty thousand people and a lobby of thirty could all be stopped by a man in a room somewhere, looking at the same image from a different angle and arriving at a truth no one else could see. It felt less like justice and more like subterfuge, a decision made offstage and delivered as fact, and yet what was the alternative, letting the wrong outcome stand because it happened at full speed?

"I don't care about the line," Genevieve said, crunching a chip. "I care that Peter's jacket almost took out the hot chocolate machine."

"It did not."

"It was airborne, Peter."

Mr. Pritchard said, mildly, "It's coming down to whether the arm was natural." His tone was so insouciant, so utterly unhurried, that Kayla's father finally turned around, as if the calm itself had pulled at him.

"They'll give it," her father said. "They always give it."

"You said that about the last one," Peter said.

"The last one was different."

The screen held its breath. The referee stood with his hand pressed to his ear, a small man in bright yellow listening to a voice nobody else could hear, and the whole lobby leaned toward him without moving, thirty people and a bag of chips gone silent. Kayla's hand drifted toward her back pocket and stopped. The letter was thin. Her father was right there, four steps away, eyes fixed on the screen. Whatever the screen said, she thought, someone in this room was about to lose something, and then after that she would show him the letter, and there would be another silence, and another kind of line drawn across a margin.

The referee lowered his hand. He looked at the linesman, then at the players, then he raised his arm and pointed to the centre circle, and the word GOAL flashed green across the screen while Peter screamed and Genevieve threw chips at him and her father turned back to the dark ice with his jaw working.

Kayla stood, and the letter crackled faintly in her pocket as she crossed the mat toward him.

"Dad," she said. "Before we go."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
story:
The hatchback was full in the wrong way, boxes where Quentin and Frank should have been, and Ashley sat with her knees against a carton of books while the town where she had lived all seventeen years shrank in the side mirror. Her mother drove. Her father navigated badly from the passenger seat, insisting the highway was the next left when it was not. Nobody had let her ride with the boxes, not even the box with the curtains, because her mother said she would just cry on them.

"Two hundred miles," her father announced, as though distance were a scoreboard.

Ashley put in one earbud and left the other out, which was the compromise she had been making with her parents all summer. She would sit in the car. She would attend the new school. She would be, as her mother kept putting it, open to it. And in exchange she was permitted to keep one thread of truculent silence running through everything, a border she refused to let them cross.

The night before, the three of them had sat on Quentin's tailgate in the church parking lot, passing a bag of gas station popcorn. Frank had said something about how they would visit, and Quentin, who was going to study psychology at the state school, had shaken his head slowly. "Visiting isn't the thing," he said. "There's this researcher, Jeffrey Hall. He did a study in 2018. He figured out that going from casual friend to actual friend takes about ninety hours together. That's what it costs. Ninety hours." Frank had said that was insane, that friendship wasn't math, and Ashley had sided with Frank, loudly, because the alternative was admitting what the number meant about the five-hour drive between her and everyone she loved.

Now, watching telephone poles tick past, she found she could not stop doing the arithmetic. She and Quentin had logged entire summers together, whole seasons of swimming and failed chemistry homework; of course they were past ninety hours, probably past nine hundred. The trouble was the other direction. At the new school she would know nobody, and every person there would start at zero, and ninety hours did not just happen. You had to manufacture them. She thought about it the way she thought about owing money: some restitution the universe expected from her, paid out in lunch periods and awkward Saturdays, and no way to skip the installments.

"Turn here," her father said, wrong again, and her mother took the exit anyway out of mercy.

Ashley took out the earbud and looked at the map on her phone, not for directions but for the schedule she had screenshotted from the new school's website before they lost signal. Chess club, Thursdays after last bell. She did not play chess. But Thursdays meant the same room, the same faces, week after week, and she understood suddenly that clubs were not really about chess, or debate, or photography. They were clocks. They were how people at a new school ran up the hours without anyone having to admit they were counting.

"You're smiling at your phone," her mother said. "That's either good or worrying."

"It's a chess club," Ashley said. "I'm signing up."

"You don't play chess," said her father, who had taught her to bicycle and to drive and nothing involving knights.

"I know." She watched a water tower slide by with some other town's name painted on it, the first thing in three states that was staying put. "It's not about the chess."

She tried to explain, and did it badly: that Quentin had told them about a study, that the study had made her furious at midnight and less furious by morning, that she had spent two years believing friendship was either there or it wasn't, some lightning you couldn't schedule, and now she was willing to consider that it was closer to a debt you paid in person. Her mother said that sounded lonely. Her father said that sounded sensible. Ashley said it was probably both and she wasn't sure the two could be neatly dichotomized, which made her father laugh for the first time since the movers came.

They crossed a state line without ceremony, just a small green sign and a change in the pitch of the road noise. Somewhere behind them, Quentin and Frank were becoming the kind of friends you text on birthdays, unless she put in the hours to keep them otherwise, unless ninety more hours, and ninety after that, could be found in holidays and a summer that hadn't been planned yet. She didn't know if that was how it worked. She only knew that she had changed her mind once tonight already, from no to Thursdays, and that a person could probably stand to do it twice.

"Fortin," her father read off a sign. "Big town?"

"Bigger than the last one," her mother said.

Ashley opened the chess club page again and typed a message to Quentin: Tell Frank he was right and also wrong. Then she looked up at the water towers and silos of the place she was going to spend ninety hours learning, and put her phone face down on the carton of books, and watched the road come.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
story:
The bus from school let them off in front of the science museum at ten past nine, and by ten Matthew was standing in front of a wall-sized printout of the Keeling Curve with his worksheet blank except for his name. The line climbed from the lower left to the upper right in a long sawtooth, jagged little teeth riding on a slope that kept rising, and above the whole thing a caption read "Atmospheric carbon dioxide, Mauna Loa Observatory." His pen hovered. The first question asked what the zigzags meant, and he had written, then crossed out, "instrument error," because the teeth looked too regular for that, and also because he suspected the worksheet would not be that easy.

Bria found him there. She had finished her own sheet, folded it into quarters, and was using it to fan herself while she gesticulated at the diorama behind them, a simulated New England forest with labeled trees and a case of metamorphic rock at its edge, pressure-scarred and folded like old cloth. "This whole hall is basically a shrine," she said. "There's even a stuffed moose. I don't know what the moose has to do with carbon."

"Nothing," Matthew said. "Probably." He was still staring at the sawtooth. Somewhere behind it, he knew, was the argument he'd had with his father in the car in March, his father saying the climate had always changed, saying it calmly, hands at ten and two, while Matthew got louder and less precise and finally said something about ice cores he could not actually explain. He had walked away from that argument feeling like he'd lost it even if he wasn't wrong, and the feeling had stayed. He wanted, this morning, to be the kind of person who could read the line on the wall and say what it meant in plain words.

Miah appeared with a sandwich from the café, half of it already gone. "You're still on question one? It's a graph, Matt. Lines go up."

"The little ones go down too," Matthew said. "Every year. Then up again. Down a little, up more, down a little, up more. That's not noise. Noise doesn't keep a rhythm." He traced one tooth with his finger, close to the glass but not touching it. "It breathes."

Bria stopped fanning. "Say that again."

"It breathes. The whole curve. Once a year."

Miah leaned in, chewing more slowly now, which meant he was thinking. He pointed at the label on the nearest tree in the diorama, a maple with a small brass plate giving its genus and species. "Okay," he said. "So what's a tree doing in April? In June?"

Matthew looked at the diorama, the green of it, and then back at the graph, and something turned over in his head like a key in a lock. "Plants take in carbon dioxide when they grow," he said. "All the Northern Hemisphere's plants, all spring and summer, pulling it out of the air. That's the dip. Then autumn comes, the leaves die and decay, and the carbon goes back. That's the rise." He said it faster than he meant to, and Bria said, "Wait, wait," and pulled him to the start of the curve again, and he walked her through one full year, dip and rise, dip and rise, his finger moving along the glass.

"But why is the whole thing still going up?" Miah asked. "If the trees give it back every year?"

"That part isn't the trees." Matthew was careful now, because this was where he'd fumbled with his father, claiming more than he could stand behind. "The sawtooth is the plants. The slope underneath is something else, and I know what the exhibit says it is, but I'd be lying if I told you I understood all of it. I know what the graph shows. I don't know everything about why." It was the first time he had said that sentence out loud, and it felt less like defeat than he'd expected.

Ms. Asante drifted past, checked their worksheets, and paused at his half-blank page long enough that Matthew thought she would lecture. Instead she read his three scrawled lines, looked at the curve, and said only, "Write that breathing part down before you forget it." Then she moved on toward the moose.

He wrote it down. Then he copied the shape of one year's tooth into the margin, the small fall and the larger rise, and underneath it he wrote "call Dad," with no punctuation after, and put the pen back in his pocket. Bria was already halfway to the gift shop, waving the folded worksheet over her head like a flag.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
story:
The gym smelled of vinegar and burnt sugar, which Olivia took as evidence that everyone else's project was a volcano. Hers was a tray of marsh soil in plastic bins, labeled Littoral Sample A through F, with a poster about salt tolerance in plants that grow where the tide reaches. She had spent three weekends driving to the coast with her mother, collecting muck in coffee cans, and now the muck sat under grow lights looking, in the fluorescent glare of the gym, like something the janitor would be filing a complaint about.

The problem was the number. Her experiment required her to know how much salt she had added to each bin, and not just in grams, because grams meant nothing to the chemistry. Mr. Owusu, who had signed her entry form, had said only, "You'll need to think in moles," and then gone to argue with someone about extension cords. Olivia had a worksheet from class and a bag of table salt with a nutrition label, and between the two of them she had produced a figure she did not believe.

"Sixteen hundred moles," said Kinley, reading over her shoulder. Kinley had a project about memory on the next table and a habit of inserting herself into crises. "You put sixteen hundred moles of salt in a shoebox of dirt."

"It's a bin."

"It's a shoebox with ambitions."

Dale wandered over from the hovercraft display, eating the pretzels he was supposed to be demonstrating surface tension with. He looked at her calculation, which ran down the margin of the poster in pencil, and he frowned at it the way he frowned at multiple choice questions, which is to say thoroughly and without result.

Olivia walked it through out loud, because that was how she found her errors. Sodium chloride, one sodium, one chlorine, so you added the atomic masses off the periodic table she'd photographed on her phone. She got 58.44 grams per mole. Then the bag. Five hundred grams of salt in the bag. She had multiplied, because multiplying felt like doing more chemistry. "Five hundred grams per mole," Dale said slowly. "Wait."

The wait stretched. Olivia looked at the number 58.44, then at the bag, then at her pencil line, and she felt the shape of the mistake before she could name it, the way you feel a stair missing under your foot. It wasn't five hundred moles. A mole was 58.44 grams of the stuff, so the bag held however many 58.44s fit into five hundred. She divided, crossed out the old figure, and wrote 8.55. Eight and a half moles in the whole bag, and she had measured out a fraction of that per bin. She checked the division twice. It kept coming out the same, which she had learned not to trust about division.

From Dale's side of the table, it looked less like a breakthrough than like a girl erasing with unusual violence. He couldn't follow the arithmetic and didn't try; what he noticed was the relief arriving in stages, first in her shoulders, then in the pencil, which stopped hovering and started writing. He'd known Olivia since seventh grade, and her moods were legible if you knew the font. He ate another pretzel and watched her redo the entire results column, which meant she'd had the salt numbers wrong all along, which meant her salt-tolerant plants had been tolerating the wrong amount of salt. He decided not to mention that.

She mentioned it herself. "The data's wrong," she said. "Every bin. I salted them for an experiment I didn't run."

"So rerun it."

"The fair is in two hours."

The judges came at ten, moving down the aisle in a slow, ominous formation, and the one with the lanyard stopped at Olivia's table and asked what she had controlled for. She heard herself say the word confounder before she fully decided to, telling him that the salt concentration had been one, and that she had caught it, and that the corrected numbers were the ones in ink. He asked how she knew how much salt she'd used. She said she'd worked it out in moles, sodium chloride, 58.44 grams per mole, and he nodded and wrote something. She could not tell whether the something was approving. Kinley, passing behind him, raised both eyebrows at Olivia and mouthed, sixteen hundred.

When the judges moved on, Olivia stood looking at her bins of coastal muck, the tide-line plants wilting or not wilting according to laws she had now partially informed them of. Dale offered her a pretzel. She took two.

"Eight point five five," she said, and ate one.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
story:
Noah had claimed the corner table by the window on the second floor of the public library, the one with the wobble in its left leg, because the assignment was due Monday and he still didn't understand what a critical lens was supposed to do besides ruin books he liked.

Sloane dropped her backpack on the chair across from him and slid a paperback across the scarred wood. "Mr. Horváth gave me this when I asked him why half the reading list is dead men and there's like one woman on it." The cover showed a room with an open window, painted in strokes so diaphanous the walls seemed made of light.

"A Room of One's Own," Noah read. "Sounds cozy."

"1929. Virginia Woolf. She argues that a woman has to have money and a room of her own if she's going to write fiction." Sloane tapped the cover twice, the way she did when she was handing him something she thought would change him. "Read the part I marked, then look at your passage again."

The passage was from Pride and Prejudice, the one where Elizabeth Bennet walks three miles through mud to Netherfield and arrives with a flushed face and dirty petticoats, to the scandal of the Bingley sisters. Noah had chosen it because he liked Elizabeth. He had written in his draft that she was independent, spirited, a free agent in a world of snobs. Mr. Horváth had circled "free agent" and written, in red, "Says who? Whose freedom, on whose terms?"

Noah read the marked pages while Sloane went to find Harmony, who was supposedly meeting them but was probably still in the mystery section, where she claimed to be "doing research." Woolf imagined a gifted sister of Shakespeare, and Noah watched her get turned away, laughed at, married off, buried without a word written down. He thought about Elizabeth's dirty petticoats, which the Bingley sisters could afford to sneer at, and about the five thousand pounds everyone in the novel kept tallying like a heartbeat.

Harmony arrived carrying a stack of Agatha Christies and sat down without apology. "Are we doing the Horváth thing? Because I did mine on Marx and it kind of broke my brain." She flipped his draft toward her, scanned it, and pulled a face. "Free agent. Noah. She has no job, no property, and her whole future is an arbitration between two guys with estates. That's not freedom, that's a negotiation she didn't get to sit in on."

"That's grim," Noah said. "She's clever. She says what she thinks."

"In a drawing room," Harmony said, "to people who could ruin her by gossip. Clever isn't the same as free."

He wanted to argue, and the wanting itself interested him, because it was Sloane's book on the table and Harmony's lens in his mouth and his own first instinct somewhere underneath, still insisting on the girl he'd admired at fourteen. He read the passage again, slowly, aloud this time, and heard things he'd skimmed past: that Elizabeth's wit was performed for Darcy's benefit, that her long walk was permitted because it defied no one who mattered, that even her refusal of Mr. Collins was framed as an eccentricity the family had to absorb or expiate through apology.

"Okay," Noah said. "So the feminist lens says she's brilliant inside a cage, and the Marxist lens says the cage is made of money, and I liked her because I only saw the brilliance."

"Both things are true," Sloane said. "That's allowed."

"But which one do I write about?" He pulled the draft toward him, crossed out "free agent," and sat looking at the red circle. "Horváth wants a position, not a shrug."

Harmony leaned over the table, and for a moment the three of them were bent over the same paragraph like conspirators. "Use both," she said. "Say the marriage market and the property system are the same machine, and Elizabeth's intelligence is what the machine can't quite grind down. Say you can't tell if Austen is exposing the machine or just surviving it."

"That's the part I can't tell either," Noah admitted.

"Then say that too," Sloane said. "He keeps telling us uncertainty isn't failure."

Noah began writing in the margin, small and fast: Elizabeth's freedom is real inside the novel and impossible outside it, which might be the point. The sun had shifted and now lay across the table, catching the edge of Woolf's painted window. Harmony opened a Christie, Sloane re-read her own marked pages, and Noah kept writing until the pen went dry. He shook it, got another from his backpack, and kept going.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
Juliette had claimed the window seat by six, before her mother could colonize it with laundry. The reading nook held one cushion, a lamp with a bent neck, and a copy of the novel Mr. Lawson had assigned, its margins already dark with pencil. On Monday he had said, in his flat way, "I don't trust your narrator. Convince me why you should." Fourteen people had laughed. She hadn't. There was a test Friday, and she had nothing.

She read the scene again. The narrator, a housekeeper named Mrs. Voss, describes her employer locking a study door and says nothing was ever kept in that room but account books. Juliette had believed her the first time through. The second time, she noticed that Mrs. Voss mentioned the locked door three times in two pages, each time more casually than the last. She wrote in the margin, why keep telling me, and then felt stupid, because the book couldn't answer.

Her phone buzzed against her knee. Elyssa: "did you figure out the Lawson thing. i have a thesis and it's one sentence." A photo followed: a sticky note reading, "Voss is lying because she's jealous." Juliette typed "that's a vibe not a thesis" and put the phone face down on the windowsill. Jealous of whom, though. Of the employer? Of whoever was behind the door? The novel gave her nothing to litigate the point with, and that was the problem. She couldn't prove anything from inside Mrs. Voss's head, because everything she had was Mrs. Voss's head.

Younes called at seven. He was doing his essay already, voice tinny through the speaker she'd propped against the lamp.

"Mine's about the door," he said. "Voss says only account books. But the kid in chapter nine says his father keeps letters in there. Two witnesses, opposite testimony."

"Which one do you believe?"

"The kid. Kids don't bother lying about furniture."

"Then your essay is just a vote." She pulled her knees up. "It's like, okay, every fact we get, she saw it, or she knows it, or she decided to say it. There's no other camera in the book. If she didn't see it, it doesn't exist for us."

"So don't trust her."

"It's not that simple. She could be right about the door and wrong about why it matters. Or right about everything and still a liar by omission." She was talking faster now, the way that embarrassed her in class. "She could tell us the truth and still be hiding it."

Silence on the line, then Younes said, "I'm writing that down, don't get mad." She hung up on him, but she wrote it down too.

Here was what she wanted to test. She opened her notebook and began copying the door scene out in a different voice, not Voss speaking, but an outside voice, one that could stand in the hallway and know what the employer was thinking while he turned the key. She wrote three sentences and stopped, because the sentences told her things Voss had never said. In her version, the employer was thinking of the letters, of his son, of a debt. The reader of her version knew all three characters' minds. The reader of the original knew exactly one, boxed inside a woman who reported only what that one character saw, knew, or chose to say. It was the difference between a keyhole and the whole floor plan. When she gave her version to Younes over the phone, he said, slowly, "Oh. You turned it third-person omniscient. That's why it feels different," and she said, "That's why," and neither of them said anything for a second, because it was strange to watch a whole novel change shape from one decision about who talks.

But the quagmire was still there, waiting, and she could feel it under the test she hadn't written. Because the omniscient version wasn't truer. It just told her more, and more could be a different kind of lie; the outside voice in her notebook knew everyone's thoughts and still didn't know whether any of them were honest with themselves. If she trusted the all-seeing version simply because it saw everything, she'd be making the same mistake as readers who trusted Voss simply because she was the one talking. She chewed the end of her pencil. Trust, she wrote, isn't about how much you're told. Then she crossed it out. Too neat. She didn't actually believe the crossed-out sentence was wrong; she believed it was unproven, which was different, and Friday was coming either way.

Elyssa texted again at nine: "changed my thesis. she's not jealous, she's loyal and that's worse." Juliette read it four times. It was better than the sticky note. It could even be right. She typed "can you prove it without leaving Voss's head," deleted it, retyped it, deleted it again, and finally sent only "maybe." Some evidence would settle it; most wouldn't; the margin of the novel was filling up with both kinds of questions now, crowded together in her small tectonic handwriting, shifting everything each time she added a line.

Her mother knocked once, opened the door anyway, and said the lamp was going off at ten. Juliette said fine. She read the door scene one last time, all three mentions of it, the casualness thickening each time like varnish. Then she picked up her pencil and wrote beneath her notes, in letters she pressed hard enough to dent the next page, "Ask Voss why she keeps saying it. Ask the door who else walked through. Wait." And she underlined, twice, the word wait.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
story:
The museum's special exhibit on the French Revolution filled two long rooms, and Sadie had commandeered the bench in the corner of the second one by ten past eleven, spreading her notebook, three library books, and a printout of Mr. Doyle's assignment sheet across the seat beside her. The assignment asked for a historiographical essay: not what happened after 1789, but how views of it had changed since 1800. She had written two paragraphs in three days, and both of them felt like quotations arranged in a row, inert as the guillotine blade under glass across the room.

She heard Jeremie and Alisa before she saw them, arguing about whether the wax figure of Robespierre looked like their vice principal. They drifted over, and Alisa leaned in to read the assignment sheet upside down.

"Historiography," Alisa said. "That's like, the history of the history."

"That's the whole problem," Sadie said. "Every book I find says the Revolution meant something different. One says it invented modern democracy. One says it was a disaster that took France decades to recover from. One guy in the 1970s apparently ruined everyone's Christmas, but the textbook doesn't say how."

Mr. Doyle had returned her draft on Thursday with a red question mark beside the paragraph she was proudest of, the one about François Furet. She hadn't asked him about it. Asking felt like admitting that the paragraph she'd built her whole argument on might be sand, and she had spent the weekend not looking at it, which was its own kind of answer.

Her grandfather was waiting in the museum café at noon, as arranged, stirring the same coffee for ten minutes because it was too hot and he refused ice. When she slid into the chair across from him, he nodded at the notebook under her arm.

"The French Revolution," he said. "I lived through some arguments about that one. Well, read about them."

"How views changed," she said. "Since 1800. Everyone agreed for ages, and then in the seventies they stopped agreeing, and I don't understand what actually broke."

"Furet," her grandfather said, as if the name settled something. "Nineteen seventy-eight. His book came out in French, then was translated as Interpreting the French Revolution. You've come across him?"

"He's the one with the question mark," Sadie said, and before she could stop herself she told him about the draft, the red mark, the paragraph where she had claimed that Furet proved the Revolution had failed. Her grandfather set down his spoon.

He didn't correct her. He just looked at her the way he looked at crossword clues he intended to solve himself, and said, "Read me the paragraph." She read it. He listened all the way through, then turned his cup a quarter turn on its saucer.

"When I was in Paris that book was everywhere," he said. "People argued about it at dinner. My host called it arrogant. His brother called it overdue. Furet argued the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history." He said it slowly, the way you hand someone something fragile. "The key to all of it. Every government since, every war, every street name. That was what he wanted them to stop doing."

Sadie didn't write anything down for a moment. Then she crossed out a line in her draft, and another, and the paragraph she had been proud of dissolved into margin scribble. Furet hadn't been saying the Revolution failed. He'd been saying it shouldn't be load-bearing, that a whole country had been leaning its entire story on 1789, and Furet had pulled the beam out to see what stood on its own. That was the break in the 1970s: not new facts, but a fight over what the old facts were allowed to mean. Her essay didn't need a verdict on the Revolution. It needed the argument about the verdict.

"Thank you," she said, already standing, already gathering the notebook.

"Sit, finish your tea," her grandfather said, but she kissed the top of his head and went back up through the exhibit, past the guillotine blade and the wax Robespierre, to the bench in the corner of the second room. She flipped to a clean page and wrote, at the top, in small letters: Interpreting the French Revolution, 1978, translated. Then, underneath: start here.

Alisa came back with two postcards and found her already writing fast, filling the page from the margin inward. "What did the old man tell you?" Alisa asked.

"More than the whole semester has," Sadie said, and kept writing.

story:
The boxes arrived at four o'clock on a Friday, and by Monday morning they had colonized the storeroom behind the kitchen at Marlowe's, stacked in front of the fire exit like a wall built by someone with a grudge against architecture. Oliver stared at them while tying his apron. He was sixteen, three weeks into his first job, and until that moment his ambitions at the restaurant had extended no further than learning where the clean rags lived.

"You're blocking the door," he said to Terence, who was rolling napkins with the speed of a man who had done it ten thousand times and resented each one.

"That's the dry goods. Nowhere else to put them. It's fine."

"It's a fire exit."

"It's a Tuesday," Terence said. "There's not going to be a fire on a Tuesday."

Oliver did not argue, partly because Terence was nineteen and partly because Oliver suspected his own objection was borrowed anyway. It had come from Mr. Ross's history class, from a Tuesday very much like this one, when Mr. Ross had put up a photograph of a burned building and said almost nothing, which was his way of making students talk.

Oliver had a shift that afternoon and a quiz that morning, so the timing felt like a kind of synchronicity, if synchronicity meant that everything inconvenient arrived together. The quiz was on the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, which happened in New York on March 25, 1911, and killed 146 garment workers. That much Oliver knew cold. What he could not stop thinking about, walking to school with his apron folded in his backpack, was the part that felt less like a date and more like a design flaw: many of the workers were trapped because the exit doors had been locked. He wrote that on the quiz. He underlined it, which was probably unnecessary.

Afterward Ahmed leaned across the aisle. "Locked doors. Why would anyone lock them?"

"Somebody in class said the bosses did it so workers couldn't take breaks or steal," Oliver said. "Mr. Ross wouldn't confirm it. He just said, what do you notice about who died and who decided."

"That's a teacher move. It's like a magician refusing to show you the trick."

"It's infuriating," Oliver agreed. "Also it works. I've been thinking about it for two days."

Mr. Ross had gone on that day to unions and strikes and the laws that came afterward, the ones about hours and doors and wages, and Oliver had half-listened the way he half-listened to most things that happened before 1950. The past had seemed like a country he would never visit. Then he had taken a job bussing tables for minimum wage, worked a nine-hour shift on his feet with one break, and discovered that the country was adjacent to his own.

At the restaurant that afternoon he mentioned the boxes again, this time to the manager, who was counting receipts and did not look up.

"It's temporary," she said.

"Everything's temporary until it isn't," Oliver said, and immediately worried it sounded like something from a fortune cookie.

"Move them yourself if you care so much."

This was clever, he had to admit. It put the labor of the objection on the objector. He moved what he could, which was four boxes, before the dinner rush swallowed him, and the wall rebuilt itself by Thursday, higher, as if the boxes had a social life he wasn't privy to.

He tried talking to the other kitchen staff. Terence was skeptical in the loud way. Ahmed, who worked at the coffee shop two doors down, was skeptical in the polite way. "My manager does the same thing," Ahmed said on a smoke break he didn't smoke, just standing with them in the alley. "Everyone says complain to the union, but we don't have one."

"Some places do," Oliver said. "There are laws too. About breaks, and hours, and exits. Mr. Ross had a whole unit on it. I zoned out through most of it, which I now regret."

"You zoned out through the unit on your own life," Ahmed observed. "That's almost impressive."

"It was the nineteenth century."

"Your legs at hour nine were the twenty-first."

Friday, Oliver did the thing that felt equal parts brave and specious in his own estimation: he wrote it down. Not a manifesto, just a dated note in the phone memo app, a photograph of the exit, and the beginning of a question, which was whether the fire code counted boxes stacked against a door as a violation or as a lifestyle choice. He emailed the city. Then, feeling exhilarated by his own audacity in a way he suspected he would pay for, he taped a polite card to the storeroom shelf: PLEASE KEEP EXIT CLEAR, and beneath it, in smaller letters, TRIANGLE SHIRTWAIST, 1911, LOOK IT UP.

Terence found it within the hour. "What is this?"

"An educational service," Oliver said.

"A hundred and forty-six people," Terence read off his phone, having looked it up with visible reluctance. "Garment workers. In New York. Doors locked." He looked at the boxes, then at Oliver, with an expression Oliver had never seen on him before, which was the expression of a thought arriving. "That's grim."

"It's a Tuesday," Oliver said.

Terence laughed, which in Terence's language was a treaty. By closing they had moved eleven boxes into the dining room corner, badly, creating a hazard the manager would surely notice, but a different hazard, and Oliver found he preferred it. He had not fixed anything, not really. The manager would have opinions on Monday, and the email to the city might vanish into an inbox forever. He was aware that his position was stitched together from a quiz and a cornered conscience, and he could not yet say whether the laws and the unions and the locked doors all connected the way Mr. Ross implied or whether that was a story adults told to make history feel orderly.

But Sunday night his phone buzzed. An inspector will follow up within five business days, the email said. Thank you for reporting.

Oliver read it twice, then held it out to show Ahmed across the counter at the coffee shop.

"Five business days," Ahmed said. "I'll believe it when I see a clipboard." But he copied the email address into his own phone, and after a moment, so did a girl from the kitchen whose name Oliver didn't know yet.

"Careful," Terence said, when Oliver told him Monday. "This is how it starts. First it's boxes, then it's demands."

"Mr. Ross says that's exactly how it started last time," Oliver said. "Also, the inspector came. This morning. Clipboard and everything."

Terence set down his napkins. "No."

"Yellow paper on the storeroom door," Oliver said, grinning. "The exit's clear. You can almost see the street."

story:
The assignment sheet lay on the kitchen table where Sebastian had left it two days ago, curling slightly at one corner as though trying to escape. Sixteen bars, Ms. Tang had written at the top in her narrow hand, with chord changes, in standard notation, due Friday. She had underlined "standard notation" twice, which Sebastian took as a message aimed at him personally, since last term he had turned in a melody notated on a napkin. He still maintained the napkin had been clean.

The house was empty until six. His mother was at her shift, his father at the depot, and the afternoon light through the living room window had gone crepuscular in that way it did in November, thin and gray, as if the sun had other commitments. Sebastian sat at the electric keyboard with the volume turned low and a stack of blank staff paper beside him, because Yahia had texted him a maxim that morning, something his grandfather supposedly always said: a problem you can't finish is a problem you haven't delimited. Sebastian had replied, "your grandpa sounds exhausting," but he'd also looked up what delimit meant, and now he was trying to apply it. Sixteen bars. Chord changes. C major, because C major was the key of people who owned exactly one keyboard and had started lessons at eleven and quit at eleven and a half.

He got eleven bars in before dinner. The melody wasn't bad, he thought, or at least it wasn't a crime. It wandered up and came back down, took a little turn in bar seven he was quietly proud of, and arrived at bar sixteen like a man reaching his own front door. The trouble was the arrival. He played the ending four times, and each time it landed flat, a thud where a click should be, and he couldn't say why. It was like shaking someone's hand and having them not look at you.

He tried things. He doubled the last note. He held it longer. He added a little leap up to a high C, which made it worse, more like the melody was showing off at a party. He texted Kasey, who had been composing since she was nine and had opinions about everything including, once, the correct way to load a dishwasher. She texted back a single word: "harmony?" and then, before he could respond, "your ending needs the chords to do something, not just the tune."

Sebastian looked at what he'd written for the final bars. C, then C again, then C, a whole skyline of C major, supportive and dull, like a friend who agrees with everything you say. In bar fifteen he had a G chord under the melody, and he knew from the keyboard's little screen that G major was G, B and D, three notes stacked like bricks. He played it into the last bar. Still a thud. He sat there in the gray light eating a piece of bread his mother would have called dinner if she'd seen it, and then he did what he later thought of as the brave thing, though at the time it only felt like fiddling. He added one note to the G chord. Just one. He put his little finger on the F above the B.

The ending changed. He played it and the last C major arrived with a pull behind it, like the F had grabbed the melody by the sleeve and said, sit down, we're home now. He played it again, louder than he meant to, one hand on the G, B, D and F and then resolving into the C chord, and the whole sixteen bars suddenly sounded like they had been going somewhere on purpose. He laughed out loud in the empty room, which he would not have done in front of anyone.

He spent the evening notating it, which was slower and less glorious. Ledger lines, stems, the dreary bureaucracy of music. He wrote the four-note chord into bar fifteen and, because he wanted to know what he'd done, searched until he found a chord chart that told him. G7. He said it out loud to the room: "G7." The chart listed the notes, G, B, D and F, and said it pulled strongly toward C major, which was the least surprising thing he'd read all week, since he had felt the pulling with his own hand.

At school the next morning he played it for Yahia in the practice room before homeroom, and Yahia, who was mostly a drummer and treated melody as a rumor, listened all the way through with his arms crossed and his chin doing a slow nod, like a man at a car auction trying not to bid. "Bar fifteen," Yahia said. "That's the one. What is that?"

"It's called G7," Sebastian said.

"You're going to say that like it means something to me."

"It has an F in it. The G chord, but with an F. And then the last chord's C and it kind of, pulls."

"Pulls," Yahia repeated, in the tone he used for weather reports and horoscopes. But he hummed the last two bars anyway, twice, and then a third time, and Sebastian watched him get it, watched the hum slow down at the F the way a person slows at the top of a hill on a bicycle.

In class Ms. Tang had them play their pieces one at a time, and when Sebastian finished she was quiet for a moment, tapping her pen against the music stand. "Bar fifteen," she said. "Whose idea?"

"Mine. Sort of. I was just trying things."

"Mm," she said, and wrote something in her book, and Sebastian spent the rest of the period wondering whether the note was praise or a suspicion that he'd stolen it. He decided he could live without knowing. When the bell rang he was still thinking about the F, about how he'd found it by accident and understood it after, which seemed like the wrong order but might be the only order there was. Yahia caught him at the door.

"Play it again," Yahia said. "The pull part. Just that part."

story:
The printer at the public library jammed on the third page, and Ryan stood over it pulling at the warm paper until it tore. His debate packet for Thursday was due to the coach by midnight, and the topic, resolved that surveillance technology does more good than harm, was the kind of thing that sounded like a philosophy seminar and felt like an argument about nothing. He needed evidence, not vibes, and the library's research databases were the only ones that didn't cost money.

He carried the crumpled page to a table by the window where Dereck was sprawled with his phone, and Andrew had his history binder open to a chapter on the Cold War. Dereck looked up and asked what was so urgent, and Ryan said he had to argue against surveillance, which Dereck found hilarious, because, as Dereck put it, Ryan had once spent an entire weekend deleting every photo of himself from group chats after a bad haircut.

"I have nothing to hide," Dereck said, thumbing through his phone. "Everything I do is boring. Let them watch."

Ryan was about to agree, because honestly his own life was mostly practice schedules and unanswered texts, but Andrew tapped his binder and said that was exactly what people said about wiretaps, and that arguments like Dereck's had been eviscerated in some court case or other, he couldn't remember which. Ms. Kaminski, shelving returns two aisles over, said without turning around that the archive terminals near the periodicals were faster than the debate sites they were probably all on, and that June 2013 was a good month to look at if anyone cared about the topic. Then she walked off with her cart, as if she hadn't said anything at all.

Ryan searched the date. The first result was a court order, and under it a news story that stopped him cold: in June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers. He read the sentence twice. Not the content of calls, the story was careful about that, but who you called and how long you talked. He turned his screen so the others could see.

"So they know Dereck called his ex for forty minutes," Andrew said.

"Seventeen minutes," Dereck said, and then, quieter, "you can know that from a list?"

That was the thing, Ryan thought, the inchoate unease he'd been trying to sharpen all afternoon finally taking a shape he could name. Dereck hadn't said anything on that call worth hiding. But a list of everyone he called, dated and timed, would tell a story about him anyway: who he was drifting from, who he called at midnight, who he never called at all. Ryan started writing on the torn printer paper, filling the margins. The good-faith version of the other side was real too, and he made himself put it down: if records like that stopped one bombing, wasn't that worth it? Pure rationalism, Andrew called it, weighing lives against privacy like units on a scale. Ryan wrote that down as well, because a good debater had to be able to eviscerate his own case before someone else did.

Dereck had gone quiet, scrolling his call log like he was seeing it for the first time. He said he still thought the whole thing was probably fine in practice, that ordinary people were too boring to matter, but he didn't say it with the same bounce as before. He asked Ryan to send him the article. Ryan said he would, and then felt strange about it, because sending an article about call records would put Dereck's number in Ryan's own call log, and somewhere, apparently, that kind of list existed whether they minded or not.

By the time the library closing announcement came over the speakers, Ryan had two pages of notes and no conclusion, and the coach would want one. He didn't have it. He had a fact, a friend who'd stopped shrugging, and an argument he actually half-believed in both directions. He decided he would stand up on Thursday and say the honest thing: that he couldn't prove the harm outweighed the good, but that anyone who claimed the trade was simple should have to hand over their own call list first.

He packed his bag. Dereck was still at the table, reading the article on Andrew's laptop now, and as Ryan walked past, Dereck looked up and said, "Seventeen minutes, man. Don't put that in your speech."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
story:
Mr. Rossi set the photocopies face down on the desks like playing cards, and Savannah watched the back of Judith's sheet as though the news might show through it. It was the last Tuesday before the oral exam, and tomorrow each of them would stand at the front and summarize, in German, a short article about a flood in a town she had never heard of.

"You get four minutes to read," Mr. Rossi said. "Then you turn it over and tell us what it says. No notes."

"None?" said Destiny, two rows over.

"None."

Savannah turned her sheet over when he clapped his hands. The article was short, maybe a hundred and twenty words, and immediately it looked wrong. Words were capitalized everywhere, not just at the start of sentences and not just names like the Weser. The River had a capital. The House had a capital. The Help had a capital. She had read one paragraph of Goethe in class and thought nothing of it, but here, in newspaper print, the capitals came in dozens, and her eye snagged on every one.

She counted them instead of reading. That was the mistake. With three minutes gone she had assembled maybe six meanings, and two of those she had guessed from a photograph of men stacking sandbags. She turned the paper over, stood, and said, "The water is very much. The people are in the houses, and the firemen come with sand." It came out flat, and Mr. Rossi's pen did not move.

"Which people?" he asked.

She didn't know. She sat down and Judith stood and did hardly better, and Destiny after her, and Mr. Rossi finally lowered the pen and said, "Again Thursday. Same article. Read it differently."

After class, in the corridor, Judith flipped her sheet back over and glared at it. "It's the capitals. They're screaming at me. Every second word looks like the start of a sentence and I keep resetting."

"No," Savannah said slowly. She was still looking at her own copy, at the shape of the sentences. "Look. House, river, helpers, sandbags. They're all capitalized, and they're all things."

"So?"

"So maybe it's not random. Maybe that's a rule." She held the sheet between them. "German capitalizes every noun, not only names. That's why it looks like this."

Judith squinted. "Every noun? Even, like, dog?"

"Look at the article. Find me a noun that isn't capitalized."

Judith found sand, street, cellar, tree, shelter, each one marching forward with its capital like a soldier. "Huh," she said, and copied the list onto her palm with a ballpoint pen.

Savannah went home and tried the theory out properly, spread on her bed with a dictionary and the flood article and a highlighter she'd stolen from her mother's desk. The rule held. It held in the caption and the headline and the quotes. And it did something she hadn't expected: with the nouns lit up, the sentence stopped being a smear of unfamiliar words. The lowercase words around them, the little words, were mostly the connective ones she already knew, the to and the in and the with, and the capitalized words in between were the load-bearing things. She could almost parse a sentence the way she parsed an English sentence, by its skeleton. She read the article three more times, then turned it over and recited it to the ceiling. "The river broke the dike on Monday night. The helpers brought sand to the old town. The mayor asked the inhabitants to leave their houses."

It was clumsy and it was hers.

Thursday, Mr. Rossi clapped his hands and Judith went first, reading with her palm of blue ink half-hidden in her fist, and did well enough that he nodded. Then Destiny, then the boy who never spoke, then Savannah. She stood, turned her sheet over, and this time she read it in two passes. First her eye caught the capitals, the nouns standing out of the line at a glance, and she let them tell her the cast of the sentence: river, dike, inhabitants, shelters. Then she filled in the small words between. The substrate of the language, she thought, the layer she kept building on, had been there all along, marked in capital letters, and she had spent three weeks resenting the marking instead of using it.

She gave the summary. "On Monday night the river rose over the dike. The water came into the old town. Many inhabitants went to the schools, because the schools are on the hill. The mayor said the helpers work day and night."

Mr. Rossi's pen moved. At the end he said, "Better. You sounded like a newspaper."

From him, that was almost a compliment, and she felt it too warmly for a second before she caught herself.

Afterward, outside, Judith caught up with her at the bike racks. "So is that it? Nouns capitalized, problem solved?"

"No," Savannah said. She was honest about it because she wanted to be, even with herself. "It tells me where the things are in a sentence. It doesn't tell me what the things mean. Tonight I'll be back at the dictionary either way."

"Then why do you look so pleased?"

"Because it's like the language is being fair. It's hard, but it shows you its hand." She unlocked her bike, then paused. "Or that's how it seems tonight. Ask me after the exam."

"Ask me too," Judith said. "I'm going to read the horoscope page tonight. All nouns, all capitals, all mine."

Savannah laughed and swung onto the seat, and pedaled off with the article folded in her back pocket, its capitals still rising out of the lines behind her eyes.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
story:
Coralie spread the biology review sheet on the flat rock by the pond and weighted its corners with four pebbles, because the wind coming off the water kept lifting the paper as if it wanted to expropriate her homework entirely. The quiz on DNA was Monday morning, first period, and Mr. Nasser had already told her that if she failed it she would be pulled from the field trip to the genetics lab in the city. She wanted that trip more than she had wanted almost anything that school year, and she was not going to lose it to a worksheet.

Koraly dropped onto the grass beside her with her own copy of the sheet, already smudged. "I got the concept," Koraly said. "Big picture. But these letters, I don't know. It's like the whole thing is written in code and nobody gave us the key."

"The key is the base pairs," Coralie said, though saying it made her aware that she was repeating something Mr. Nasser had written on the board rather than something she actually understood. She looked at the reeds along the far bank and then back at the page. "In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine. Guanine pairs with cytosine. That part I have."

"Then why do you keep staring at question four like it insulted you?"

Question four gave a DNA template strand and asked for the RNA that would be transcribed from it, and then for the amino acids that RNA would code for during translation. Coralie had written out her answer twice, and both times Koraly had circled something and said it looked wrong, and both times Coralie had said Koraly was wrong, and now neither of them was sure of anything. The sequence was A, T, G, C, C, A, and Coralie had transcribed it as T, A, C, G, G, T.

Carson arrived with a fishing rod he had no intention of using, which everyone knew, and sat on the end of the dock with his shoes off, his feet in the water. "You're supposed to be quizzing each other," he called. "That's the whole reason I came. Entertainment."

"You're the entertainment," Koraly said. "Feet in the pond like a tourist." But she turned her sheet around and read question four aloud to him anyway, slow, letting him hear the letters.

Carson dragged his feet through the water, thinking. He was canny about test questions in a way neither of them was, the kind of student who read the directions twice and caught the word "except" hiding in the last line. "It says RNA," he said. "You wrote RNA?"

Coralie looked down. She had copied the strand letter for letter, swapping each base for its partner, and she had put a T in the second position where the DNA had an A. She had done the same in the sixth position. The rest of the class period on Thursday, Mr. Nasser had said the words "in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine," and she had written them down, and then she had ignored them completely.

"The RNA can't have any T in it," she said slowly. "That's the mistake. Both times. In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine, but in the RNA, adenine pairs with uracil instead. So every A in the template, I have to answer with U, not T."

"Say the whole thing," Koraly said. "Because I still don't get why."

"There's no why on the sheet. It's just the rule." Coralie took out a fresh pencil. "In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine. In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine." She wrote the corrected strand: U, A, C, G, G, U. The third position had stumped her too, until she checked it against her notes. G in the template meant C in the RNA, and she had that one right both times, which was something. "The first part, transcription, is just copying the DNA into RNA with that one swap. Then translation is when the RNA gets read in threes and each three makes an amino acid, and the amino acids chain up into a protein."

Koraly copied the corrected strand onto her own sheet, letter by letter, mouthing it. "So my eye colour, all of it, that's a phenotype, and it started with this? Letters?"

"It's the protein doing something," Coralie said. "The letters are instructions for the protein. I don't know it past that yet." She said it without embarrassment, because it was true, and because she had decided over the past hour that pretending to a completeness she didn't have was how she had gotten the T wrong in the first place. She had trusted the shape of the answer rather than the actual rule. Mr. Nasser kept saying the exam would test exactly this, the switch, the small substitution that changed everything downstream, and she had nodded along.

Carson stood up on the dock, dripping, and pointed at the shallows where a frog sat on a lily pad, still as a painted thing. "That frog," he said. "Everything about it. That all came from the letters."

"More or less," Coralie said. She folded her sheet along its crease and put the pebbles in her pocket. There were questions she could not yet answer, like what told the cell where to start copying, and she would look those up tonight, but the core of it sat in her hand now, small and exact. She could recite the pairs forward and backward. She did so, once, quietly, while the frog held its position in the reeds.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
The screen door at his grandfather's house still slammed the way it had when John was ten, and the same tin of peppermints sat on the windowsill above the sink. He had come for the last week of August, carrying The Great Gatsby in his backpack because his college roommate assignment email had mentioned a first-year seminar, and the syllabus began with it. His grandfather had read the book decades ago and forgotten everything except that he'd disliked it, so when John mentioned the seminar, the old man proposed a club. "We'll meet on the porch," he said. "I'll provide lemonade and objections."

Marko and Niko were already at the lake for the weekend, and they biked over the first evening, sweating, arguing before they even dismounted. Marko wanted to study business in the fall and read the novel as a manual for getting ahead; Niko, who was deferring a year, had read it twice and considered it a tragedy about class. The four of them sat in the wicker chairs with the book open on knees, and the argument went nowhere until Marko found the sentence he'd underlined. "Nick says, 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.' Straight from the narrator, page whatever. So he's trustworthy."

"Published in 1925," Niko said, "and you think the narrator's honest just because he says so." He leaned forward and started listing, counting on his fingers. "Nick says he reserves all judgments, then judges everyone within two pages. He doesn't tell anyone that Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle. He quietly arranges Gatsby's funeral and then paints himself as the only loyal one left. He claims not to care about Jordan and then can't stop watching her." Marko pushed back, then conceded a point, then pushed back again, and John sat mostly silent, turning his glass, feeling the two positions collide somewhere in his chest without merging.

His grandfather, who had been listening with his eyes closed, opened them. "When I was in the mill," he said, "the foreman used to tell us he never favored anybody. Said it every payday." He drank his lemonade. "Took us a year to see the shifts he handed out." He didn't draw the conclusion; he just set the glass down on the porch rail, and John felt the remark catalyze something that had been forming all evening. If a narrator insists on his own honesty, that insistence is itself a piece of evidence, and it has to be weighed like any other.

John went inside and got the notebook he'd been using to prepare for the seminar. In chemistry that spring he had loved the unit on enthalpy, the idea that every change carries a hidden ledger of heat absorbed or released, and he wrote at the top of a fresh page: every claim by a narrator has a hidden ledger too. He listed what Nick hid, what Nick revealed, and then, more slowly, what the point of view made possible. Because the story came only through Nick, Gatsby stayed a myth; nobody could check him. The reader's trust wasn't in Gatsby, John wrote, it was in Nick's account of Gatsby, and Nick had shown them he bent accounts.

On the porch the argument had shifted. Marko admitted the narrator was "shady, fine," but argued that made the book better, not worse: "You have to do the work yourself." Niko said that was generous to a man who let a woman take the blame for a death, and for a moment the word malevolent hung in the air, Niko applying it to Tom Buchanan, Marko objecting that Tom was careless more than evil, careless in the way careless rich people are. John listened to both and found he could not fully join either. Nick was dishonest and also the reason anything beautiful survived on the page; the claim of honesty and the lying seemed to feed each other rather than cancel out.

His grandfather's own want surfaced later, when the others had biked home in the dark. He helped John carry the chairs in, and in the kitchen he said, offhand, that the club could meet again tomorrow, and the day after, since everyone was around until Sunday. John understood then that the book had been a pretext, or at least half of one, and that his grandfather had spent the evening not arguing but being in a room full of voices. He felt a small ache about this, thinking of the quiet that would return after John left for college in twelve days, and he said, "Tomorrow works," and watched his grandfather's face do something it tried not to do.

Before bed John sat at the kitchen table with the notebook open, adding one more line to the page. What stayed uncertain, he wrote, was whether Nick knew he was lying, and whether that mattered more or less than the fact that the lies were lovely. He read the sentence over twice, decided he'd keep it for the seminar even if it made him sound unsure, and closed the notebook. Through the window the lake was a black rectangle with one dock light burning at the far end, and upstairs, in the old man's room, a radio came on low, tuned to the station that played until midnight.

story:
The guitar had belonged to Lucas's grandfather, and it arrived at the music classroom in a cardboard box that smelled of someone else's house. Mr. Zhao had agreed to open the room after school on the condition that Lucas put it back on the rack himself and swept the rosin off the floor. The strings were dead, grey where a person's fingers had worn them, and none of them held a pitch for more than a minute. Lucas turned the tuning pegs and watched the needle on his phone app drift flat, drift flat, drift flat, as if the instrument were deciding against him.

"You're fighting it," Fatoumata said from the doorway. She had her violin case with her, as always, and she set it on a chair without opening it. "You tune up, then you let go."

"Up?"

"Below the note, then up to it. Tighten, don't loosen." She came and stood beside him. "My teacher calls it recuperating the string. You go past the note and come back, and then it holds."

Lucas tried it. He dropped the fat string low, wound it slowly upward, and the needle steadied on E. He plucked it again. Still E. Something in the instrument seemed to settle, the way a locked jaw settles when you stop forcing it. He wrote nothing down, but he said the letters to himself under his breath, the order Mr. Zhao had made the whole class memorize in September without ever saying why: E, A, D, G, B, E. Lowest to highest. He had assumed it was trivia then, something extrinsic to actual playing, the kind of fact that existed only to be tested. Now it was a map, and every peg was a country he had to name before he could cross it.

The second string gave him E as well, which stopped him cold. He plucked the low one, then the thin one. Same letter, two different sounds, one deep as a cellar and one thin as wire. He turned to Fatoumata, and before he could ask, Nour was in the doorway, late, still in his gym clothes.

"It's the same note," Lucas said. "The first and the last. E and E."

"So it repeats," Nour said, dropping onto the piano bench. "So what?"

"It doesn't repeat, it's an octave apart, I think. Look, I'm not explaining it, I'm telling you what the app says." He held the phone out, and Nour waved it off, but Fatoumata leaned in and looked at the screen for a long moment, and the three of them stood in a small triangle around the dead grandfather's guitar while the late sun came through the blinds and cut the room into stripes.

Nour picked out "Smoke on the Water" on one string with his thumb, badly, and Fatoumata told him to stop, and he didn't, and she took the violin out of its case and played one clean high note that made them all flinch. "That's what your high E wants to be," she said. "Yours is close. Your B is the problem." She was right. The B refused, the needle sliding sharp no matter how slowly Lucas wound. He loosened it below the note, came back up, and it went sharp again, and he began to understand that the guitar was not going to be tamed in one afternoon, that the strings would stretch and slip and need retuning tomorrow, and the day after, for weeks.

He had wanted, when he carried the box through the hallways, something simpler than this. A guitar meant something, or he had thought it did, some image of himself at a party with the thing across his knee and everyone quiet. That version was extrinsic too, he realized, a reward that had nothing to do with the object itself. The real thing was this: a dead instrument, a borrowed room, two friends killing an hour, and six letters in an order he now knew by feel as much as by memory. He wasn't sure which version he actually wanted. Probably both. Probably that was the honest answer, and he let it stand.

Mr. Zhao put his head in at four o'clock. "Lockup in ten." He looked at the guitar, at the tuning app still open on the stand, and didn't offer anything. Lucas went back to the B string. He dropped it low, felt the slack, wound up in half-turns, listening more than watching, and the needle crept toward the letter and held there, trembling, for three plucked notes before it slid sharp again.

"Tomorrow," Fatoumata said, snapping her case shut.

"Tomorrow," Lucas said, and slid the guitar into the rack, B string still bright and wrong.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
story:
The laminated map had been in Thomas's backpack for three days, folded against a thermos, and by the time he spread it on the sand it had taken on a soft crease down the middle of the Atlantic. Nigel crouched beside it, shielding his eyes. Behind them the beach ran out in a long shallow curve, and Mr. Haddad was already down by the waterline with his coffee, pretending not to supervise.

"Explain it to me," Nigel said. "The whole thing. If you can do it here, you can do it in the exam room."

Thomas had wanted this since October, since the day Mr. Haddad had put a question back to the class, why is it that London sits at the same latitude as Newfoundland yet its winters are mild, and Thomas had said nothing. He had known pieces of it then. He had not been able to hold them together in front of thirty people. That silence had stayed with him like a splinter, small and located precisely.

He traced the coast of Florida with one finger. "Warm water leaves the Gulf, runs north along the American side. Fast, deep, narrow. That's the Gulf Stream." His finger moved out past the bulge of Newfoundland, beyond the Grand Banks, out into the open grey of the mapped ocean, and there he hesitated, because the arrow he was following thinned and the label changed.

"You've stopped," Nigel said.

"The same water," Thomas said slowly, "but past the Banks it isn't called the Gulf Stream anymore." He looked at the legend, then back at the drifting arrows. "Beyond the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, its continuation toward Europe is called the North Atlantic Current. Or the North Atlantic Drift. Same thing, two names."

"Then why does the map act like they're different currents?"

Thomas had asked himself the same thing at his desk on Tuesday, shading the water with a pencil until the page went dark and smudged, and his mother had come in and asked what he was drawing and he had said weather, and she had said the sea again, and there had been something in her voice, pride and worry braided together, that he had decided not to interpret. He was leaving in September. Six hours away by train, to a city where the ocean would be a different colour. Maybe he was trying to take this ocean with him, foldable, portable.

"Names are what people put on water," he said. "The water doesn't know them."

Mr. Haddad had drifted up the beach by then, sandals in one hand. He didn't sit. He only said, "So tell Nigel why England isn't frozen," and then he waited, in the way he waited, which had once seemed cruel and now seemed more like patience with sharp edges.

Thomas put his whole hand flat on the map, palm over the Atlantic, fingers spread toward Europe. "This warm water carries heat north and east. When it reaches Europe, the wind coming off it is milder than it has any right to be at that latitude. That's why their coasts are warmer than ours at the same distance from the pole." It came out steadily. Nigel was nodding, actually nodding, and Thomas felt something loosen in his chest that had been clenched since October.

"So the warm current," Nigel said, "is like a heating pipe running across the ocean."

"I used to think that," Thomas said. "I liked that picture, actually. A pipe, a conveyor, everything fixed." He looked out at the actual water in front of them, which was not cooperating with any map: the foam came in at one angle and the gulls wheeled against it at another, and a thread of kelp moved sideways along the shore, going nowhere either toward or away from them. "But look at it. It's all eddies, all this turning and losing itself. The map makes it look like determinism, like the water has no choice but to end up warming Dublin. The real thing is more like weather. You can name it and you can trust it, mostly, and you can't ever fully pin it."

Nigel squinted at the map. "Then why learn it at all?"

"Because it's the best true thing we have," Thomas said. "It's not the whole truth. It's the part that holds still long enough to say." He was aware even as he said it that he was talking about more than water, and he let that stay unspoken, the way the Gulf Stream, past the Banks, keeps moving under a borrowed name.

Mr. Haddad finished his coffee and looked at the horizon as if grading it. "The boy who wouldn't answer in October," he said, mostly to the sea. He turned to walk back down the beach and then paused, without turning around. "You'll do. Tell your mother she's emancipated from driving you to tutoring."

Thomas laughed, and then caught himself on the word, that was the wrong word, rescued entirely, and he was still deciding whether to correct Mr. Haddad when a wave came up farther than the others and slid cool across his ankles, soaking the hem of his jeans. He grabbed for the map but Nigel had already lifted it clear, holding it up to the light, and the sun came through the lamination and lit the arrows from behind so that they glowed, evanescent, almost not there. "So it changes its name in the middle of the ocean," Nigel said, "and you're sure about which part is which?"

"Not sure," Thomas said, wringing out his cuff. "Confident." He took the map back, folded it along its old crease, and started up the sand toward the boardwalk, where his mother was waiting in the car with the engine running, having driven him here after all.
